problems.title: Maximum Subarray
problems.statement: Given an integer array nums, find the contiguous subarray with the largest sum and return its sum.
problems.understanding: The key question at each position: is it better to extend the current running sum, or start fresh? Discarding negative prefixes is the locally-optimal choice that gives the globally optimal answer.

naive.title: Naive Solution — Brute Force
naive.html: Try every possible subarray. For each starting index, scan right and track the running sum.

problems.intuition: At each index, either extend the previous subarray or start a new one. If current + nums[i] < nums[i] the prefix actively hurts us — discard it. This is Kadane's Algorithm (also a 1-D DP recurrence).
problems.approach:
1. Initialize current = answer = nums[0].
  2. Iterate i from index 1 to end.
  3. At each step: current = max(nums[i], current + nums[i]).
  4. Update answer = max(answer, current).
  5. Return answer.
problems.takeaway: Pattern — Kadane's Algorithm — Start fresh when the prefix becomes a liability

problems.title: Jump Game
problems.statement: Given array nums where nums[i] is the maximum jump length from index i, return True if you can reach the last index.
problems.understanding: All we need is whether the end is reachable — not how. At each index track the furthest position currently reachable. If we reach an index that exceeds our current reach, it's impossible.

naive.title: Naive Solution — Brute Force
naive.html: DFS from index 0: try every valid jump length recursively.

problems.intuition: Scan left-to-right maintaining farthest — the furthest index reachable so far. If i > farthest at any point, we are stranded.
problems.approach:
1. Initialize farthest = 0.
  2. Iterate i from 0 to end.
  3. If i > farthest: return False (gap in reachability).
  4. Update farthest = max(farthest, i + nums[i]).
  5. After the loop, return True.
problems.takeaway: Pattern — Furthest Reachable — greedily extend the reachable frontier

problems.title: Jump Game II
problems.statement: Given nums, return the minimum number of jumps to reach the last index. It is guaranteed you can always reach the end.
problems.understanding: Think of each jump as a BFS 'level'. Within the current jump's reach, find the position that extends the frontier farthest. When we exhaust the current level, increment jumps and start the next level.

naive.title: Naive Solution — Brute Force
naive.html: DFS trying all jump lengths from each position, tracking minimum jumps.

problems.intuition: Greedy BFS: treat each jump as expanding to the next 'level'. Within the current range [prev_end+1 … current_end], find the furthest reach. When i == current_end you must jump — increment and extend.
problems.approach:
1. Initialize jumps = 0, current_end = 0, farthest = 0.
  2. Iterate i from 0 to n-2 (last index never needs a jump from it).
  3. Update farthest = max(farthest, i + nums[i]).
  4. When i == current_end: increment jumps, set current_end = farthest.
  5. Return jumps.
problems.takeaway: Pattern — Greedy BFS Range — current range → next range (BFS compressed, no queue)

problems.title: Gas Station
problems.statement: Given gas[i] and cost[i] for a circular route, find the starting station index from which you can complete the full circuit (or return -1).
problems.understanding: If starting at s causes a fuel deficit at station i, then no station between s and i can work either — they inherit the same or worse prefix. Jump directly to i+1.

naive.title: Naive Solution — Brute Force
naive.html: Try every station as a start, simulate the full circuit for each.

problems.intuition: Two insights: (1) A solution exists if and only if sum(gas) >= sum(cost). (2) Whenever running fuel goes negative, every station from start to i is invalid — skip them all and try i+1.
problems.approach:
1. If sum(gas) < sum(cost): return -1 immediately.
  2. Initialize start = 0, fuel = 0.
  3. Iterate each station i: add gas[i] - cost[i] to fuel.
  4. If fuel < 0: set start = i + 1, reset fuel = 0.
  5. Return start.
problems.takeaway: Pattern — Greedy Candidate Elimination — failed range means every start in it is invalid

problems.title: Hand of Straights
problems.statement: Given an array of card values hand and an integer groupSize, return True if you can rearrange all cards into consecutive groups of size groupSize.
problems.understanding: The smallest available card must start a group — there is nothing smaller to put before it. Greedily consume groups starting from the minimum each time.

naive.title: Naive Solution — Brute Force
naive.html: Sort, then repeatedly remove groups starting from the smallest element using list.remove().

problems.intuition: Use a frequency map. Iterate sorted unique keys. For the smallest key with count > 0, try to consume frequency copies of each of the next groupSize cards. If any is short, return False.
problems.approach:
1. Return False if len(hand) % groupSize != 0.
  2. Build count = Counter(hand).
  3. Iterate first in sorted(count).
  4. Skip if count[first] == 0.
  5. Set frequency = count[first].
  6. For each value in [first, first+groupSize): if count[value] < frequency return False; subtract frequency.
  7. Return True.

optimal.title: Optimized Code (Python 3)
complexity: Time: O(n log n) — dominated by sort of unique keys

problems.takeaway: Pattern — Frequency Map + Sorted Keys — always start from the smallest available card

problems.title: Merge Triplets to Form Target Triplet
problems.statement: Given a list of triplets and a target triplet, you can merge any two triplets by taking the element-wise max. Return True if you can form the target.
problems.understanding: Merging uses max(), so any triplet where one coordinate exceeds the target can never be used — it would permanently overshoot that coordinate. Filter those out and check if the remaining triplets collectively cover every coordinate of the target.

naive.title: Naive Solution — Brute Force
naive.html: DFS trying all subsets: include or exclude each triplet, merge, and check against target.

problems.intuition: Discard every triplet where any coordinate exceeds the target (merging would lock us above target). Among the remaining valid triplets, check whether we can find the exact target values at each coordinate position.
problems.approach:
1. Initialize found = [False, False, False].
  2. For each triplet: if any triplet[i] > target[i], skip it entirely.
  3. Otherwise, for each position i: if triplet[i] == target[i], set found[i] = True.
  4. Return all(found).
problems.takeaway: Pattern — Greedy Filtering — eliminate impossible candidates (those that overshoot), then verify coverage

problems.title: Partition Labels
problems.statement: Given string s, partition it into as many parts as possible so that each letter appears in at most one part. Return the lengths of each partition.
problems.understanding: Once a character appears in a partition, every later occurrence of that character must be in the same partition. Knowing each character's last occurrence lets us greedily expand a partition's boundary until it becomes self-contained.

naive.title: Naive Solution — Brute Force
naive.html: Scan partitions naively: expand each window until no character inside it has a last occurrence outside the window.

problems.intuition: Pre-compute last[char] = last index of each character. Scan left-to-right. As we see each character, extend end to at least last[char]. When i == end, a self-contained partition is complete.
problems.approach:
1. Build last = {char: index} for last occurrence of each character.
  2. Initialize start = 0, end = 0.
  3. Iterate i, char in s.
  4. Update end = max(end, last[char]).
  5. When i == end: append end - start + 1 to result, set start = i + 1.
  6. Return result.
problems.takeaway: Pattern — Last Occurrence + Greedy Boundary Expansion — extend window until it is self-contained

problems.title: Valid Parenthesis String
problems.statement: Given string s containing '(', ')', and '*' (where '*' can be '(', ')', or empty), return True if it is valid.
problems.understanding: Instead of branching on every '*', track the range of possible open-parenthesis balances: [low, high]. high < 0 means even the most optimistic interpretation is invalid. low == 0 at the end means there's at least one valid interpretation.

naive.title: Naive Solution — Brute Force
naive.html: Backtracking: try all three interpretations of each '*' recursively.

problems.intuition: Track a range [low, high] of possible open balances. '(' increments both. ')' decrements both. '*' shrinks low and grows high. If high < 0, definitely invalid. Clamp low at 0 (balance can't go below 0 in any valid string).
problems.approach:
1. Initialize low = 0, high = 0.
  2. For each char in s:
  3. '(': low += 1; high += 1.
  4. ')': low -= 1; high -= 1.
  5. '*': low -= 1; high += 1.
  6. If high < 0: return False.
  7. Clamp: low = max(low, 0).
  8. Return low == 0.
problems.takeaway: Pattern — Balance Range [low, high] — track the window of possible states instead of every individual state
